subject: toucan
pitch: A keel-billed toucan showing off on a short mossy branch. A huge rainbow beak in lime green, sky blue and orange with a cherry-red tip, a glossy black body, a lemon-yellow bib, a ring of lime-green skin around each eye, bright blue feet and a scarlet patch under the tail. A single pink orchid blooms on the branch beside it.
reasoning:
I'm sketching proportions for a keel-billed toucan model—roughly 0.5m total with a 0.3m body and 0.15m beak, perched on a branch at floor level, and working out the branch's radius and placement.

I'm placing the orchid stem off to the side, then mapping out the bird's upright posture with loft stations from tail through hip and chest up to the neck, head, and beak tip coordinates. Now I'm defining the skeleton hierarchy with root, spine chain, neck, head, jaw, tail, legs, and wing chains to keep the rig organized but not overbuilt.

Writing skeleton chains...

Still defining leg joint chains...

Writing toe sprout calls...

For wings, I'm deciding on a slightly spread, angled-out-and-back pose rather than fully folded or fully extended, defining a joint chain from shoulder through elbow and wrist to tip to give a semi-open "showing off" look.

Mapping out the trailing edge polyline points to build the wing membrane, pairing them against the leading edge chain with matched weights, and keeping the color dark near-black for the skin.

For the body, I'm deciding to loft it as a sweep bound to the tail-spine-neck bone chain, now defining the station points (position, width, height) along that path.

I decide to simplify bone assignment to just spine, neck, and tail for the body loft. Then I turn to coloring the bird, planning a paint function that creates a yellow bib on the upper chest using position and normal direction checks with a smoothstep for soft blending.

I work out the bib's shape using a radial distance calculation centered near the throat, scaling x and y differently to get an oval boundary, then blending yellow into black at the edge and adding a paler cream rim near the top to approximate the toucan's real coloring pattern of white throat, yellow bib, and red under the tail.

For the red undertail patch, I'm considering whether to paint it directly on the body surface based on position and normal direction, or add a separate small ellipsoid part near the tail base for a simpler, more visible scarlet patch.

Since materials are shared and matte, I'm thinking about adjusting roughness after construction by traversing the model and lowering roughness values for a slightly glossier finish, then moving on to placing the head sphere.

Now I'm positioning the head geometry and working out eye placement, with a lime-colored ring around each eye and a black pupil, trying to figure out the best way to stick a flattened ring shape onto the curved head surface using an oriented cylinder.

Now designing the beak as a tall curved shape swept along a path from the base inside the head to the tip, tapering the radius down with a curve function so it narrows and flattens toward the point.

I'm working out the coloring scheme for the keel-billed toucan beak, using the surface normal and position along the beak to blend bands: lime green along the top ridge, orange through the middle, and blue along the lower edge, smoothed with gradients based on height.

Adding tip and base details...

I'll scope painting to just the body, upper and lower beak, and the mossy branch, skipping the orchid petals. Now I'm working out the geometry so the lower mandible sits snugly beneath the upper beak's tomium line, calculating the center and radius at each z-slice to keep the gap consistent.

I'm hitting a snag near the tip though—the upper beak's bottom edge and the lower beak's top edge seem to cross over each other instead of meeting cleanly, so I need to adjust the curve values there.

Now I'm setting up rigging: the lower mandible gets its own "jaw" bone separate from the "head" bone, connected at a joint, and I'm defining the radius functions that taper the beak's width and height along its length, checking the math at the midpoint to make sure the curve shrinks smoothly toward the tip.

For small details, I'm adding dark nostril dots near the base and deciding to skip serrations and a top decal ridge, but adding a casque-like ridge sweep along the upper beak surface in a yellowish-green tone with a small radius, plus a darker band near the base via vertex paint.

For the tail, I'm planning flat sweeping feathers along the tail chain, tapering in width and getting flatter toward the tip, colored black, with the local frame oriented so the normal points sideways relative to the tangent.

Keeping the tail solid black rather than adding color variation, same for the back and belly, then starting on the branch sweep with a mossy coloring.

For the branch's structural anchor, I'm reconsidering the joint hierarchy—rather than forcing it onto the bird's existing root, I'll make a dedicated "root" joint at the branch base and parent the bird's pelvis to that, so the branch acts as the stable foundation and the bird sits on top of it.

Working out the branch geometry itself: I'm sweeping a tapered tube along the path with mossy coloring, making sure the radius and center heights keep the lowest points resting right at y=0 so nothing floats or clips oddly.

For the moss paint, I'm blending a brown bark texture with patchy green moss on top using noise and smoothstep based on the surface normal's y-component, so moss appears more on upward-facing surfaces and bark grain shows through elsewhere.

For actual moss tufts, I'm thinking small scattered low-poly icosahedron clumps across upward-facing branch surfaces rather than relying on texture maps, since SVG/canvas texturing needs a document context I don't have here. I also want to add a side twig sprouting from the branch's right end.

Now I'm placing a single pink phalaenopsis orchid beside the bird, built from a bark-colored twig stem with an arching bloom made of rounded petal and sepal shapes -- two large upper petals, three sepals, and a central lip -- oriented to face the viewer.

Placing petal geometries...

I'll offset each petal's z slightly to avoid z-fighting, add a green calyx sphere behind the flower at the twig tip, and sketch in two flattened ellipsoid leaves near the branch base with their own position and scale tweaks.

Now I'm orienting the petal/leaf parts using the dir/axis convention so local z aligns along a given direction, then adding a couple small pink buds further along the arched stem before finalizing where the flower attaches at the twig tip.

Adding more buds along the stem... I realize the orchid's x position overlaps with the bird's right wing when it extends outward, so I need to reposition the orchid to the other side of the branch to avoid collision.

Finalizing orchid flower center and leaf positions with the shifted branch span, and keeping the bird centered near x=0. Now I'm detailing the wing membrane chain coordinates for the shoulder, elbow, wrist, and tip joints, naming each segment for the skeletal hierarchy under the spine.

I need to make sure the mirrored wing geometry doesn't produce inverted normals -- since the right and left sides are mirrored, the winding order of the membrane faces could flip and cause backface culling issues, so I should swap the edge order for one side to keep both wings rendering correctly.

With DoubleSide the rendering should flip correctly for backfaces, so I'll apply that to all materials rather than just wings. For the wing coloring, I'll skip fancy noise gradients and just go with plain black wings with some gloss for simplicity. I'm also sanity-checking proportions—body width around .11-.12 at the chest, comparing shoulder position against wing placement to make sure the loft sizes line up.

Now I'm working through leg geometry: hip, knee, and foot joints positioned so the short toucan legs sit mostly tucked under the belly with just a small visible shank, using a tapered sweep for the leg chain. I'm checking that the toes land just at or slightly below the branch surface so the feet appear to grip rather than float above it.

Checking the midpoint distance from the branch axis confirms it clears the surface fine, and the ankle sits safely above the branch with proper clearance for the toe radius.

Now I'm setting up the toe sprouting logic — each toe grows from the ankle joint to its tip using a small radius taper, with color passed through sweep options and a "digit" role tag. I'm naming joints by position, like toeF1L for front-left toe one, keeping the zygodactyl pattern of two toes forward and two back for the toucan's foot.

For the body coloring, I'm adding a cream/yellow throat patch as a small ellipsoid under the chin, separate from the head sphere, to mimic the toucan's pale bib area that extends up toward the face.

Writing bib paint logic...

Still working on beak coloring...

Adding a dark tomium line along the lower edge. I'm checking the body's overall geometry: the tail chain branches off separately from the torso path and sweeps down behind the branch, verifying it clears the branch's height so there's no collision.

Now I'm defining the sweep geometry for the tail — tapering radii along binormal/normal axes with rounded caps, setting up the frame orientation so tangent, normal, and binormal stay consistent. Then I'm wiring up the skeleton rig, parenting the spine chain to the pelvis joint and building out the spine and neck chains point by point.

For the head, I'm sweeping the beak along a catmull-rom smoothed path rigidly attached to the head bone, using explicit weights so it stays rigid rather than deforming with nearby joints.

I'm using rounded caps on both ends of the beak, with roughly 8-10 sided cross sections and slightly flattened proportions (rx smaller than ry) for a natural look, then adding small nostril spheres positioned just off-center near the top of the upper beak.

Now I'm calculating eye placement against the curved head surface -- figuring out the x-offset at the target y/z coordinates using the head's ellipsoid radii, then checking whether the eye disc's cylinder radius will protrude past the curvature or sit flush against it.

Fixing the glint position so it sits just above the eye, and matching head and body colors to the same dark base shade so the paint looks consistent. Now I'm thinking about scattering small icosahedron mossy tufts across the branch surface for added texture.

For moss placement, I'm sampling points on the branch sweep geometry, filtering by surface normal to keep tufts facing upward, and embedding small randomized icosahedrons with varied coloring. Then I'm traversing the whole model to adjust material roughness for a consistent matte look, settling on a compromise roughness value since the branch and body share the same painted material.

Now I'm working out the orchid flower region, positioning it with a bone attachment and computed orientation, then defining each part—petals, sepals, lip, column, calyx—using shared sphere geometry with distinct colors and scaled thinness for a flattened petal look.

Placing the dorsal sepal, lateral petals, and lower sepals with specific offsets, scales, and z-rotations to tilt each one outward naturally based on which side it's on.

Now I'm positioning the lip, its tip, and the column with their own scales and colors, then checking how the Region's local frame and `at` option resolve through the explicit root bone weighting.

I'm adding the two orchid leaves as elongated ellipsoids pointing in mirrored directions off the root bone.

The branch itself curves from roughly x=-0.34 to x=0.28 using a catmull-rom path with a tapering radius function, rounded at the left knob end, plus a small broken stub rod near the right side in matching bark color.

Now I'm setting up the skeleton joints: root at the base, pelvis parented to root, with each createJoint call checking parent hierarchy and default orientation. For the wing chain, I'm defining the membrane surface between the leading and trailing edges using an array of path points, with scalloped edges and a set thickness.

I'm defining a shared sheen paint function that mixes dark navy tones based on surface normal, reusing it across the wings, tail, and body so the coloring stays consistent, while keeping the body's underside bib as a separate paint pass.

For geometry, I'm sharing a sphere mesh for plain-colored parts to avoid unnecessary allocation, and setting up small icosahedron shapes for individual fur tufts that get scaled per instance.

I'm scattering tuft hit points across the surface with distance filtering and a slight upward normal constraint, then working out the beak ridge's curve path for the mesh.

Checking the math, the ridge center and radius values don't line up with the upper beak profile, so the ridge would float off the surface. Rather than fixing the ridge geometry, I decide to drop it as a separate sweep and just suggest the keel shape through coloring instead, since getting consistent upper-path centers and radii would take more rework than it's worth.

Looking at the beak proportions, it's currently too tall relative to the head -- a real beak base is closer to the head's own height. I'm adjusting the upper beak to be bigger with larger rx/ry, and reworking the lower beak's center and radius so it sits properly below the upper base without gaps.

Still tuning beak curve points...

Checking the beak proportions against head geometry, the length looks right at roughly .14 protrusion. I'm now setting up the sphere helper function and the mirror loop for symmetric left/right parts before writing the final code.

Writing leg sweeps...

Then I'll finalize by baking the root mesh and traversing it to return the complete model.
